speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has decided to appoint an Advisory Committee on Parliamentary Salaries and Expenses. This committee will be asked to undertake an independent and impartial review of the financial arrangements made for members of both chambers of Parliament, including the Speakers, ministers, and other members receiving additional emoluments for special duties. It will be asked to report any immediate changes it deems appropriate, as well as a procedure whereby future revisions may be undertaken from time to time.
The membership of the committee reflects experience from a number of different viewpoints in the community. The Chairman will be Mr. T. N. Beaupre, the President of Domtar Limited, and a former Assistant Deputy Minister of Defence Production. The other members will be Mr. Arthur Maloney, the former Member of Parliament for Toronto Parkdale, and Mr. Marc Lapointe of Montreal, who has been active on behalf of organized labour in industrial relations matters.
In recent years there has been a good deal of discussion of the question of the remuneration of elected officials. This is not a problem that has been limited to the Canadian Federal Parliament. In recent months the legislatures of both Ontario and Quebec have increased their indemnities. In the United Kingdom and the United States, however, legislative remuneration was revised only after independent commissions had examined conditions and all relevant considerations, and had reported.
The government believes that if any revision in the financial provisions is called for, such revision should be based upon an impartial analysis of conditions by persons outside elected ranks, experienced in levels of compensation in other sectors of the community. The people of Canada, no doubt, wish their representatives to be provided for in a manner that will enable them to devote themselves principally to public service. It is hoped that the report of this advisory committee will provide a better understanding of the financial arrangements necessary to a proper discharge of these duties.

I for one have always regarded with some approval the system which has prevailed in the United States for some time where a commission of nine members, three appointed by the President, two each by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, by the Vice-President as presiding officer of the Senate, and by the Speaker of the House of Representatives, from outside the ranks of the congressional group, examine in an objective way and without being subject to any accusations of self-interest, the whole issue of the salaries and other benefits which must be accorded to those involved in the democratic life of that country.
I think something of this nature is long overdue and so far as I can see, Mr. Speaker, it is the only way there can be any degree of acceptance throughout the country for a periodic review of the issues raised by the President of the Privy Council.

speechtext:

The reception procedure requires that the inmate he:

(e)	Assessed by the supervisor of education to determine academic and vocational needs.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Regina East, to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the program announced by the Minister without Portfolio in charge of the Wheat Board on February 27 and the immediate threat it poses to the livelihood of 190,000 prairie farmers, together with the failure of the government to develop programs to ensure a basic income for farmers in western Canada, such discussion being immediately necessary because no legislation is to be presented on the subject and farmers must make vital decisions within the next few weeks.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext:
The hon. member has given the Chair the notice required under Standing Order 26. In saying this, I think I should mention that unfortunately the notice was misdirected and did not come to the attention of the Speaker except by a circuitous route, which perhaps delayed consideration of the
Inquiries oj the Ministry matter by the Chair. In any event, the Chair has had an opportunity to consider the proposal contained in the suggested motion.
I can tell the hon. member, and all hon. members, that this is a decision which is very difficult to take. I have considered all aspects of the matter and I am still wondering whether the motion should be put to the House or not. Hon. members know that under the provisions of paragraph 5 of Standing Order 26, the Chair must have regard to the probability of the subject being brought before the House within a reasonable time by other means. I know how important this matter is to Canada in general and to the wheat growers and the economy of the west in particular. However, the Chair still has to take into account the question whether it is probable that this very subject might be brought before the House within a reasonable period of time.
I have never made it a rule that if there is to be a supply motion within a reasonable period of time this should necessarily be the vehicle for discussion of a matter referred to in a proposed motion under Standing Order 26. Nevertheless, this aspect cannot be entirely overlooked. There is also the fact that the budget will be brought down in the very near future, and this will provide a vehicle for consideration of this matter of urgent national importance. Even with this taken into account, I am still not convinced that the hon. member should not be given the benefit of the doubt and allowed to proceed with the motion.
Standing Order 26(6) makes it possible for the Chair to delay a decision for a short while until later in the sitting. If hon. members would permit, I should like to reflect further on all aspects of this matter, particularly on whether there is a possibility of this urgent problem being brought before the House for debate within the next few days. Having taken these factors into account the Chair might make a decision, perhaps at five o'clock, on whether or not there should be a debate this evening on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar. So the decision will be held in abeyance and made known to the House later this afternoon. Oral questions.

That in accordance with section 19 of an act respecting the status of the official languages of Canada, chapter 54, Statutes of Canada, 1968-69, this House approves the appointment of Keith Spicer, Esquire as Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, by way of explanation of the background of the motion perhaps I might read into the record the relevant provisions of section 19 of the Official Languages Act adopted by Parliament in the last session. Subsection (1) of section 19 provides and I quote:
(1)	There shall be a Commissioner of Official Languages for Canada, hereinafter in this act called the Commissioner.
Next is the most germane clause. Subsection (2):
(2)	The Commissioner shall be appointed by commission under the Great Seal after approval of the appointment by resolution of the Senate and House of Commons.
Subsection (3) provides:
(3)	Subject to this section, the Commissioner holds office during good behaviour for a term of seven years, but may be removed by the Governor in Council at any time on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The purpose of the motion therefore, Mr. Speaker, is to comply with the requirement of the Official Languages Act and to request the approval of the House, as the approval of the other place will be requested, to the appointment of Mr. Spicer to this position under the Great Seal of Canada.
Mr. Spicer is a native of the city of Toronto, having been born there in 1934 and having been educated in the elementary and secondary schools of that city. In terms of post secondary education he holds: 1. Diplome d'etudes de civilisation frangaise, Sorbonne, Universite de Paris, 1955; 2. B.A. in Modern

Languages and Literatures, University of Toronto, 1956; 3. Diplome de l'lnstitut d'E-tudes Politiques, Universite de Paris, 1958; 4. Ph. D. in Political Science, University of Toronto, 1962. He has been in the academic profession having taught at the University of Ottawa for four years; the University of Toronto for three years, where he had been in the position of Associate Professor and is now Special Lecturer on French Canada; was visiting professor for one term at Dartmouth College in the United States and this year is visiting Associate Professor of Political Science at .Glendon College, York University.
In addition to his academic occupations Mr. Spicer was active as Organizing Secretary of Canadian Overseas Volunteers in 1960-61, an organization which members will recall was one of the constituent organizations of what has since become Canadian University Students Overseas, or CUSO; in the summer of 1964 Mr. Spicer served as Staff Researcher on the Armed Forces, Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism; in the years 1964-65 he was known in this building as the Special Assistant to our late colleague, the Honourable Guy Favreau, then minister of justice and subsequently president of the privy council; during the years 1966 to 1969 he served as an editorial writer with the Toronto Globe and Mail and during that time had some leave of absence for academic purposes. Then, between the years 1961-69 he served as a commentator on the French network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, broadcasting in French in the International Service of that corporation in 1968-69.
In terms of publications Mr. Spicer has published frequently on the question of external aid. In the spring of 1961 he published in the International Journal an article on "The Administration of Canadian Colombo Plan Aid"; in June, 1962, in Volume 5 of Canadian Public Administration he published "Quelques problemes des experts techniques Canadians a l'etranger", and in the International Journal in the winter of 1969-70 there appeared his article entitled "Clubmanship upstaged: Canada's 20 years in the Colombo Plan". Those who have studied Canada's foreign aid program will recall Professor Spicer's monograph which was the subject of his doctorial thesis, "A Samaritan State?- External Aid in Canada's Foreign Policy," published in 1966.
Mr. Spicer is married to a former native of France and has a family of three children. In the opinion of the government he would be

an apt representative of English Canada, with extensive studies in French language and French culture, to carry out the very important function which this Parliament has assigned to the Commissioner of Official Languages. On that basis, the government has put forward this proposal, that his nomination might be approved.
Mr. R. Gordon L. Fairweaiher (Fundy-Royal) Mr. Speaker, we are in the middle of a very important consideration of a very important appointment, and I am grateful for the opportunity to speak for the official opposition about the appointment of Dr. Keith Spicer. As the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) told us, the nominee has a most impressive academic record. I am sure that, coupled with this record, are the essential qualities of sensitivity and open-mindedness which will be so necessary for carrying out this worth-while task for Canada. I hope that the Commissioner designate will heed the need for a very early reassurance to the public servants who have been deeply troubled about their future because of what I might categorize as the rather ill-considered and flip statements made by certain people.
For 103 years, Mr. Speaker, we have been engaged in an experiment in nationhood called federalism. The years have been punctuated on occasion by stridency and shrillness uttered by negative men whose vision of what Canada can be is obscured. Fortunately, other men have understood the stresses and tensions of our evolution. We must reinforce the original and imaginative concept of confederation to fix today's period of profound readjustment. Northrop Frye has reminded us that nations have followed their uncreated ideal. I believe this is very true of this country. He says this at Page 122 of his book:
The Canada to which we really do owe loyalty is the Canada that we have failed to create ... I should like to suggest that our identity, like the real identity of all nations, is the one that we have failed to achieve. It is expressed in our culture, but not attained in our life, just as Blake's new Jerusalem to be built in England's green and pleasant land is no less a genuine ideal for not having been built there. What there is left of the Canadian nation may well be destroyed by the kind of sectarian bickering which is so much more interesting to many people than genuine human life. But, as we enter a second century contemplating a world where power and success express themselves so much in stentorian lying, hypnotized leadership, and panic-stricken suppression of freedom and criticism, the uncreated identity of Canada may be after all not so bad a heritage to take with us.

I sincerely hope, and I say this on behalf of my Party, that Professor Keith, Spicer will help to bring reality closer to the ideal.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF KEITH SPICER AS COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even though I have had the pleasure of meeting Dr. Spicer briefly, it is impossible for me to say exactly what his qualifications are for this particular position; but I am, as are my colleagues, prepared to accept the judgment of those who chose him. He is certainly a man of great culture and, what perhaps is more important, he possesses a great sense of humour which he will probably need in performing his duties.
It has taken us more than a century to do what perhaps ought to have been done on the first day of Canada's birth, establish the notion that bilingualism is part of our national culture and national being. When the Commissioner approaches his job of making bilingualism a reality in federal institutions and the various language districts to be set up under the Act, I am sure he will remember that it has taken us a century to come this far, that during the course of the century a great many anomalies, injustices and disparities in language among groups in Canada have developed, and that those disparities and anomalies cannot be erased over night. He must remember that setting the record straight and overcoming the difficulties and conflicts which have arisen in the course of a century will require a great deal of patience, diplomacy and sensitivity, because his work will touch on the lives, security and confidence of a good many Canadians.
If he remembers that, Dr. Spicer will have an opportunity of making bilingualism in Canada a living thing and there will be no bitterness or recrimination from any section of the country. On the other hand he can act, as I hope he will not, like a bull in a china shop by trying to make things accord to his view very quickly and thereby produce a great deal of resentment and bitterness which will take another century to erase. I therefore urge, as I have in past debates on this Bill, that Dr. Spicer, whom I do not know very well, display a sensitive, open-minded, patient and diplomatic approach to the problems he will encounter.
He has considerable powers under the Act, not as great as some hon. members have suggested, but very great nonetheless. He will be the recipient of many complaints from people who think that English or French has been ignored and by people in the federal public service who think that our emphasis on lan-

He will receive a good many complaints from people who have a real grievance and, I suspect, even more complaints from people who have no grievance at all but who are either deliberately or unconsciously out to create mischief. It will be a measure of his greatness as a human being and not merely as one who is a recipient of a doctorate if, at this time when Canadians are aware of the conflicts and divisions within their society, he will approach all these complaints fairly and perform his duties with an unremitting determination to face Canada's present and future difficulties and build the foundations of greater unity.

speechtext: that Bill S-20, an Act respecting the labelling, sale, importation and advertising of consumer textile articles, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) for giving me the opportunity of introducing this bill in the House. I hope I shall be equal to the task.
It is a privilege and pleasure for me today to present Bill S-20, entitled an Act respecting the labelling, sale, importation and advertising of consumer textile articles. Of the many problems consumers face in making an informed choice in the market place, none is more complex than the problem of selecting between textiles. Not only are consumers concerned with the fibres being used in textile articles, but they are also concerned with the care of such products, the availability of adequate sizing, and other important facts such as wearing qualities, including serviceability. A pre-requisite to judging these factors is to know the fibres from which the cloth and textile products are made.

March 2, 1970
Textile Labelling Act
However, the activities of the department have not been restricted to this one objective. As members know, a sizing program for children's clothing has been introduced, and it should revolutionize the sizing of children's garments. As a logical extension of that program, and one which consumers have requested, is the initiation of work to provide a size system for women's clothing.
In the matter of care labelling, I hope shortly to announce a system which will greatly assist consumers in the care of garments. However, as I have indicated, the complete success of such programs requires the creation of a viable system for the identification of fibres and this bill will provide the cornerstone.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
In terms of these objectives, I am certain that passage of this bill will be welcomed by all consumers in Canada. It is particularly gratifying to be associated with legislative action designed to alleviate some of the problems and frustrations faced by everyone in today's market-place.
I believe we will all agree that the most deserving beneficiaries of this bill will be the women of this country who largely bear the responsibility for purchasing the family requirements in clothing and other household articles. While we may be reluctant to acknowledge the fact, I think that the majority of the male members of the House might privately confess that a great deal of reliance is placed upon the knowledge and instincts of their wives when it comes to the selection of quality in their clothing requirements.
I am delighted to recognize the initiative shown by the member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) in bringing forth a private member's bill relating to mandatory labelling of textiles. The text of his bill indicates a parallel concern regarding the plight of the purchaser of textile articles and I am certain that he will find that the provisions of the present bill are in accord with his own objective.
The Canadian textile industry generally supports a move to bring more order to the manner in which both imports and domestically produced articles are labelled. Deficiencies in labelling are prevelant in both categories, to the detriment of the more conscientious firms who endeavour to maintain a high level of informative labelling. Since the requirements for mandatory labelling called for in this Act apply equally to
[Mr. Lanelois.l
imports and domestic production, this inequity will be removed and all will compete on the same terms.
It is evident from the provisions of the bill that retailers will derive protection comparable to that supplied to the consumer by the requirement that the label be applied by the supplier of the finished article. Although the mandatory labelling is geared mainly to the consumer's needs, the implementation of the regulations under this Act will help the retailer and manufacturer to minimize complaints and returns.
Textile fibres, and the textiles and clothing made from them, rank as one of the three major essentials of man. We all are consumers of textiles and it is estimated that each of the memibers present in the House is wearing at the moment approximately 4 to 5 pounds of consumer textile products of the kind which will be subject to the proposed legislation. In 1969, Canadians used in excess of 700 million pounds or approximately 33.5 pounds per capita and it is estimated that the total value of products subject to the provisions of this Act is approximately $1.4 billion annually.
In recent years, the industrial progress and technical advancements which have been achieved in the chemical and textile fields have brought immeasurable benefits to consumers. In providing a much broader range on man-made and synthetic fibres, these advancements have improved our way of life through the introduction of many modern innovations from wash-and-wear clothing to indoor-outdoor carpeting.
However, these developments have been accompanied by a proliferation in textile terms and fibre trade names which has vastly complicated the task of the consumer in making intelligent selections of fabrics and proper assessments of fibre properties on today's market.
The consumer has always been familiar with the generic names of the natural fibres, e.g. wool, cotton, linen and silk, and has not had much difficulty in learning the inherent properties of those fibres which determine the performance and care of these products. I mentioned previously the remarkable technological developments in man-made fibres. Such evolution is the main reason why the share of the natural fibers on the market has dropped from 82 per cent in 1950 to 64 per cent in 1968; a substantial amount of these natural fibres was offered under the form of blends with artificial fibres. The evolution of
March 2. 1970



the textile industry in the direction of multifibre and multi-process sophistication has placed the average shopper in an awkward position.
The price of progress has been that the consumer is confronted and often confused in the maze of man-made fibres. As a matter of fact, they are offered for sale under a multitude of trade names-Arnel, Antron, Avisco, Avril, Nylex, Nypel, Nytelle, Fortrel, Verel and Qiana. This list can easily be expanded since there are over 2,000 trade names for man-made fibres known in the textile trade. The use of some trade names may be helpful since some are now household words, but many more are not.
The present regulations in this field prohibit mislabelling and protect the consumer from fraud to this extent, but there remains a major gap where no information is offered. The only legislation with respect to the labelling of fibre content is the Regulations respecting the Labelling of Textile Materials (P.C. 1955-1515) and Regulations respecting the Labelling of Hosiery (P.C.	1962-1239) as
amended by P.C. 1964-517, both passed pursuant to Section 5 of the National Trade Mark and True Labelling Act.
Labelling of the products is not mandatory under the provisions of the existing regulations. They are based on the approach that a dealer does not have to label his product at all, but if he does, the labelling must be accurate in accordance with the regulations. Another inadequacy is that the use of the natural, chemical, technical or trade name whether such name is a registered trade name or not is permitted. While there are manufacturers who do label informatively, this generally happens only when there is a competitive advantage in doing so. In many cases those articles which are labelled do not bear the percentage for fibre blends and designations of man-made fibres are often by trade names.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As I have indicated, the proposed bill is a response to the requests and needs of not only the consumers, but also of the manufacturers and retailers of textile articles. By providing this legislation, the government is assuming a leading role in ensuring the right of the consumer to be informed of the material composition of textile products which he purchases. The buyer who has difficulty in identifying fibres by the feel of the fabric offered at the retail level, will be greatly assisted by this legislation. The Act will also guard the consumer against unfair and deceptive trade 21701-57
Textile Labelling Act
practices. The vendor or the dealer, as defined in the Act, will be required to provide the information which will help the buyer to make a knowledgeable purchasing decision. Mandatory labelling will increase the effectiveness of the consumer's choice by informing him more fully about quality, and consequently about performance and care. The provisions relate not only to wearing apparel, but also to yard goods, upholstery, wigs, carpets, floor covering, sleeping bags, draperies and other household textile items.
One of the main provisions of the new legislation is that fibre designation shall be by generic names. Possibly some of the more knowledgeable purchasers are aware that fibres sold under various trade names such as Dacron, Terylene, or Fortrel are actually of the same chemical composition and are generically named Polyester. But I wonder how many of them would recognize as the same generic Polyester fibre, those that are now sold on the Canadian market under such names as Avlin, Diolen, Encron, Forcel, Kodel, Nycron, Talan, Teijan, Tergal, Teritol, Terlenka, Tetoron and Trevira. The advantages and simplicity in the proposed use of the single generic name Polyester are obvious. The generic names for man-made fibres which will be defined in the regulations are acrylic, modacrylic, polyester, rayon, acetate, saran, azlon, nytril, nylon, rubber, spandex, vinal, olefin, vinyon, metallic, glass and anidex. The requirement for use of generic names will not prohibit the use of fibre trade names in which the owners have a large investment and a great deal of pride. The regulations will provide for the non-deceptive use of fibre trade names provided that they are accompanied by the generic name of the fibre.
While some of the proposed generic names may be unfamiliar to many consumers at this time, it will be much easier for the consumer to become familiar with the characteristics of 17 generic fibres than it has been to cope with hundreds of trade names in the past. It is recognized that there will have to be an intensive educational effort to familiarize the buying public with the significance of the generic names, and my department will meet its responsibilities in this respect.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should mention that the consumer textile market and the textile technology in Canada are very similar to those in the United States.
Because of the large volume of trade occurring between the two countries, it is desirable that the regulations adopted in Canada be

March 2, 1970
Textile Labelling Act
consistent with those of the United States. This will be largely achieved by adopting in Canada the same generic names for fibre classification. All man-made fibres marketed now under a multitude of trade names may be classified within one of 17 generic groups which will be defined in the regulations under this Act. Each group covers a class of fibres differing significantly from those in the other groups in chemical composition as well as in certain other characteristics such as washabil-ity, resistance to light and serviceability.
The provisions of the bill now before us will require mandatory labelling of prescribed consumer textile articles to disclose by generic names all fibres constituting five per cent or more of the total fibre content. In addition, the disclosure will be expressed in terms of percentage for each constituent fibre. Further provisions prohibit any false, misleading or deceptive representations being used in association with any textile fibre product by means of a label or advertisement.
Other basic provisions embodied in the bill relate to offences, penalties and disposition of article upon conviction; powers for enforcement by inspection, seizure and analytical evidence; and authority for Governor in Council to make regulations relating mainly to the technical and operative areas. This structure will provide the flexibility required to keep the regulations up-to-date with technological advancements and provide the consumer with meaningful information and protection.
I have no doubt that this Bill will considerably narrow the communication gap existing now between the consumer and the manufacturer of textile products, and that it will provide for a more orderly, informed and efficient marketplace. I trust that the objective of the government in this complex field and the bill which provides the means of achieving it will commend themselves to the House.
That this is perhaps not an idle hope is indicated by the private bill on this subject standing in the name of the member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and the general and particular interest indicated by members of all parties to see that the consumer maintains his rightful place in the market.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Lan-glois) for the efficiency and competence with which he discharged his duties and gave us the information he had received. However, I

must also deplore the fact that the minister responsible for that measure is again absent from the House.
It would seem that the ministers are now delegating to subordinates the duties which fall to them. This is an undeniable proof of the ministers' contempt for the House since they give us the impression that they find it boring here. I think this is deplorable.
Mr. Speaker, during his remarks the Parliamentary Secretary said that the bill intended to control the labelling, sale and imports of products.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
About the first aim, he spoke at length. About the second one, that is to say sales, he spoke also but we would have liked very much to hear him talk about imports. Indeed, textile imports into Canada have increased and are still increasing, which has for consequence to deprive of their jobs Canadian workers who certainly deserve more attention from the government.
As I listened to the hon. member who spoke before me, I felt as it the textile industry had just been born. I had indeed the feeling that he was laying the foundations for a new industry in Canada. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the textile industry is one of the oldest in Canada. It is steadily losing ground nowadays because of the apathy, lack of interest and scorn of this government.
Mr. Speaker, you may feel that I am out of order, but when we are talking about imports, we cannot be limited to what is happening in Canada. As a matter of fact, it is absolutely necessary to ask where they come from and what are their evil effects. As a member representing a riding where the textile industry is of vital importance, I can only bitterly and severely criticise the Liberal members. They are responsible for the stagnation in which the textile industry finds itself.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but he will agree that the bill under consideration deals only with the labelling, sale, importation and advertising of consumer textile articles, in order to inform the public about the quality of the products he is buying, and does not deal with the textile trade, either domestic or foreign.

Mr. Speaker, I will not have a polemic with you. However, I should be granted at least the same latitude as my hon. friend.
March 2, 1970



Since I must limit the scope of my remarks as much as possible, I would first tell the House and particularly the Parliamentary Secretary, that this measure is a smoke screen. Actually, the government does not wish to make known openly its inertia, its lack of foresight and also its intention not to do anything to help the Canadian workers.
The textile industry is one of the oldest in Canada and deserves better attention and protection from the government. Labelling has fooled a great number of Canadians. Importers and some foreign manufacturers took advantage of it and managed to label their products so as to cheat the Canadian buyers.
Several times in the past I have drawn the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to anomalies in and violations of the law and it seems that this has been to no purpose. It was acknowledged that there was dumping, that Canadian workers were handicapped by it. It took too long to make the necessary inquiries. It only extended the time to the prejudice of the Canadian workers who lost their jobs because of too many imported goods.
I wish to point out that there are too many textile products entering the country. I could not repeat that often enough, because some of my former fellow workers have lost their job on that account, and this government has failed in its duty.
Here are a few remarks made by companies involved in the import market. They manufacture fibres and sweaters and they ask for more protection from the government.
I shall quote a few of them:
Fibre and sweater manufacturers gave the Tariff Board a very dismal picture of the situation and spoke as late as yesterday of sales lost to imports from countries where manufacturing costs are very low.
Further on it is said:
The Canadian Chemical Producers Association has stated that the steady increase in imports of knitted garments has had an unfortunate consequence on the Canadian synthetic fibre industry.
Another party concerned says, and I quote:
Dupont of Canada Ltd., which operates the only plant in Canada producing such fibres, stated before the inquiry commission that imports from Asian countries had caused the share of the Canadian market to drop to 19 per cent in 1969, as against 75 per cent in 1965.
What is the result of this? Those 2 million pounds, comprising sweaters, have become 10i million pounds, and most of the increase benefited foreign importers.

Textile Labelling Act
Mr. Speaker, this government should have taken the necessary measures long ago. On many occasions, I myself asked questions to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and he had promised to conduct an inquiry and table the relevant report in the House in December last. We are still waiting for the conclusions of the study and, in the meantime, many Canadian workers are losing their jobs.
The government cannot plead ignorance in this matter. We of the opposition parties have warned it on numerous occasions. Those involved in the textile industry have time and again informed the government that action in this field was mandatory.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I regret, once more, to interrupt the hon. member, but he will certainly agree that his speech has no relation whatsoever to the bill now before us, which deals with labelling-

Mr. Speaker, I was about to say that because of inaccurate labelling-you were premature, whereas if you had waited a few moments more you would have known what I was going to say-people involved in the textile industry have informed the government that something should be done. The government has always postponed action from week to week, to the detriment of Canadian workers.
Mr. Speaker, although this legislative measure is far from perfect, although it is but a huge smoke-screen to make us forget the inertia of the government, we welcome it. We hope it will improve somewhat the lot of those who have been associated with the textile industry throughout their lives. I wish the parliamentary secretary all the success he hopes to achieve, for the government as well as the department certainly need it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to the speeches of the two previous speakers.
I want to congratulate the parliamentary secretary (Mr. Langlois) on his well written speech, on its delivery, and on his ability to cover the whole subject of textiles.
I also want to congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) for his efforts towards helping the textile workers.
I should very much like to continue my speech in French, but I cannot do so for two reasons: first of all, the English minority must

March 2, 1970
Textile Labelling Act
be heard in this debate; and also, I am unable to express myself as clearly and forcefully as I believe I can in English.

The purpose of this bill is to provide for regulations governing the sale, labelling, importation and advertising of consumer textile articles. Products that come under the bill will include such textile articles as clothing, fabrics sold in the piece, sheets and other household articles. The legislation would apply whether these items are made in Canada or imported from elsewhere.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
As the Parliamentary Secretary has pointed out, there are very many trade names for these manmade fibres and the labelling of textile articles is going to be a difficult and complicated matter. The bill will prohibit a dealer from selling, importing or advertising a prescribed consumer textile unless it is labelled according to its textile fibre content and in accordance with the regulations under the bill. Other provisions will prohibit misleading, deceptive and false statements being used in the sale, importation or advertising of textiles. There are penalties. A dealer violating the bill's requirements will be liable to a maximum fine of $10,000 and a person violating the provisions or regulations of the act will be liable to a maximum fine of $3,000, imprisonment for up to a year or both. What the bill does is provide that labels show on a prescribed article the generic name of each textile fibre comprising 5 per cent or more of the total fibre weight of the article.
The Parliamentary Secretary indicated when he spoke that this bill was also supported by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson), who has a similar private bill on the Order Paper. As far as that hon. member's bill goes I know he is very definitely concerned about these consumer problems and the bill is to be commended, up to a point, as is this measure. However neither one of them in my opinion goes far enough. This is not merely my opinion, but is the opinion of the one Canada-wide consumer organization, the Consumers' Association of Canada.
Like the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard), I am sorry that the minister did not show sufficient concern for the feelings of the consumers either to be here today or to explain why he could not. I think there must

be some very good reason why he is not here to listen to the discussion on this bill. I wish he had stated it before he left. I think it is important that he should be here. I also think it is a little unfortunate that he had to choose the beginning of consumer week, which today is, to introduce this bill, since it is very definitely accepted as only a half-way measure by the Consumers' Association of Canada.
Indeed, I want to give you some points expressed in a release issued on February 20 when the Consumers' Association of Canada was made aware of the contents of this bill. They expressed great dissatisfaction with the textile labelling bill which was given first reading in the House of Commons. This release states in part:
The bill is a "halfway measure" said Dr. H. Edward English, Acting CAC president. "While it seems to cover many problems encountered by consumers and will at least give basic fibre content information, consumers will not know how to clean textile articles they purchase," Dr. English continued.
That is the end of that quote, but not the end of the release which continues:
The nation-wide consumer organization originally asked textile manufacturers to state fibre content and care instructions on all textile items. When the industry took no action, CAC asked the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for legislation.
I am sorry to say that the CAC turned in vain to the government for the whole of what they wanted. They are getting labelling on fibre content but this bill does not require labelling instructions for the care and cleaning of textiles once they have been purchased.
Anyone who has looked after clothing or household articles knows it is of utmost importance, with all the variety of fibres in the articles of clothing and for the household that we are buying, to know the method of cleaning and caring for them that is required. Unfortunately, while the minister has included fibre content in this bill in respect of labelling, he has turned a deaf ear to the pleadings of the CAC that there should be labelling as to care and cleaning of the textile. So, it is not with any great degree of satisfaction that the CAC or the consumers across this country welcome this measure. We will, of course, support it and we will try to make it better when the bill is before the committee, but this is very definitely a half loaf; I am not sure that it is not the small half of the loaf at that. I know that this is an Irishism and that each half should be the same, but there is such a thing as a smaller half, and this may be the small half we are getting.
March 2. 1970

I have been led to believe that the Canadian government Care Specifications Board has already prepared specifications for the care and cleaning of textiles. These could have been included in this legislation, had the minister been prepared to do so. I should like to know why he did not. If these specifications for care are ready, why are they not included in this bill? If they are not ready, why could this measure not have been put aside for a little while until they were finally prepared and included?
I think these are very important questions and I am coming to a possible answer in a moment. This is what the consumers of Canada want in this legislation. They want legislation to provide labelling of the fibre content and also legislation to provide labelling for the care and cleaning of textiles. As I say, they are only getting a small half of their request.
According to the association, what the CAC would like is a series of simple symbols which would indicate at a glance how a material should be cared for as far as ironing, bleaching, hand washing or machine washing is concerned. Surely, that is not too much to ask. They want to know what they should do in order to look after and have looking well what they have bought. They want to know how material should be cared for as far as ironing, bleaching, hand washing and machine washing is concerned.
Let me ask again why the government is demurring? Why is it not doing this since we-I say we because I am a member of the Consumers' Association of Canada-have requested this? I have already suggested one possible reason. The one reason I have suggested is that perhaps these specifications for care and cleaning are not yet ready. That is not a valid reason because this bill could have been delayed for a little while.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I suggest there is another reason. When you go over this bill, you are rather inclined to believe that in drafting it the minister was far too concerned with the opinion of the textile manufacturers rather than with that of the consumers of this country. I think that this realization recalls the warning which I gave in this House over and over again when this department was being set up, that if you put consumer and corporate affairs within the same department you would have a built-in conflict of interest and the consumer would get the short end of the stick. I believe that
Textile Labelling Act
this bill is showing up such a conflict of interest; it is considering the convenience of the manufacturers rather than that of the customers and housewives, who are the consumers all across this country.
The proof of this I believe is that the minister has made it abundantly clear that he is not in favour of making compulsory regulations to be observed by the manufacturers. He wants to do as he does with his Prices and Incomes Commission, bank heavily on moral suasion. I do not believe that in this day and age of complication, moral suasion will suffice. I am afraid that if the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) were to have his way, he would go down to the corner of Wellington and O'Connor, rip out the traffic lights, and say,, "Let us have moral suasion to direct the traffic across the street. Everybody should restrain themselves, and moral suasion will direct pedestrians and cars alike". Perhaps the pedestrian might have the theoretical right of way, but the other fellow would have the truck, and it would not do much good to be right if you were dead.
In the matter of the labelling of textiles and other consumer problems, we have come to the stage where not the textile manufacturers, who are only a relatively small section of the community, but the consumers, that is all of us, should be given the right of way- although not all the right of way either. That is where the stop lights come in. If you instal traffic lights, then both the consumers and the manufacturers will have rights which will be regulated. I am all for the consumers; other people are all for the textile manufacturers. If we had compulsory regulations and compulsory labelling throughout, not only for fibre content but also for care of the product, we would know in what respects the consumer had rights and to what extent we had to respect the rights of the manufacturers. If this labelling is left to the voluntary co-operation of the manufacturers, they will either not do it or they will do it so halfheartedly that the consumer will not have the protection of proper labelling.
What I am suggesting is a system of traffic lights-a green light, a red light and an amber light in between to prevent collisions. This is what we need, and this is why I want to see proper regulations under this legislation. We should not leave labelling up to the manufacturer, as the minister wants to do.
I do not want to make a great production of this. I want to say that the Consumers' Association of Canada has been urging this type of

March 2, 1970
Textile Labelling Act
protection for many years. I should like to read their resolution on this subject which emanated from their latest convention which was held not long ago. The following resolution came to them from the Ontario Branch of the CAC and the Prince Edward Island Women's Institute. It was passed by the CAC. It reads as follows:
Whereas the multiplicity of textile fibres and trade names and methods of fabric construction and finish makes intelligent purchase of textile products almost impossible, and Whereas the above factors make care, laundering and dry cleaning of textile products increasingly difficult for both the consumer and the dry cleaner and,
Whereas sound information is seldom available at the time of purchase, therefore Be it resolved that CAC request the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to establish regulations-
That is not moral suasion.
-requiring that textile products be labelled with the generic name of the fibre or fibres, trade name and basic care information and that the label be permanently affixed, in a readily accessible place, to the product or its container.
That was passed by the CAC, which is the only Canada-wide consumer organization. Unfortunately, it does not have the membership it should have, and I for one would like to see it many times its present strength. Just this morning, in a television program here in Ottawa, I heard the minister say that he would like to have many Ralph Naders in Canada to protect the interests of the consumer and to bring pressure on his department to do things that needed doing. I suggest to him that he begin at home with the Consumers' Association of Canada. When they make a reasonable request he should consider it and turn a deaf ear to the textile manufacturers, realizing that this matter affects many more people than they and that he is legislating for the majority of the Canadian people Who are the consumers of this country. I urge that he either withdraw this bill or amend it in committee to add to it the labelling, care and cleaning of textiles. I will serve notice right now that if he does not bring in such amendments in the committee, then I will.
We do not have any Ralph Naders in Canada unfortunately, but in the meantime I will settle for a good CAC that will put pressure on the minister for something that we need and that is worthwhile. So we shall support this bill up to the point where we can come up with something to improve it. I guess we will have to pass it anyway, but like the CAC we will not be happy with it unless the
IMrs. Maclnnis.]
changes that are required, and that have been requested for so many years, are made.

Mr. Speaker, while the bill we are now considering does not suggest any answer likely to settle the conflict now prevailing in the textile industry, it still has some good points. I regret, however, it was not brought before the House a few years earlier.
When we consider, for instance, imports into Canada from 1964 to 1967, we realize that we have lost a significant part of the textile market.
Our industries have lost a rather substantial percentage of the market. The bill now before us will somehow help us to make up for the errors of the past and to compensate for the losses incurred in favour of countries that take advantage of circumstances to export to Canada without any valid reason.
Obviously, it is rather important to control the labelling, sale and advertising of consumer textile products. I am not a textile expert. When I happen to visit a store where such products are displayed, many times I simply try to find out from where the materials come without knowing exactly what they are made of.
The bill now under consideration, if the government does everything in its power to enforce compliance with its provisions, will be to the advantage not only of the consumers but also of the Canadian workers who rely upon the textile industry for their living.
No doubt the time had come for the introduction of a similar bill simply because every day and every week changes occur in the manufacturing methods of the textile industry.
This industry perhaps develops faster than many others in the world. Changes occur very rapidly. Therefore, it has become very difficult for the consumer to be in a position to know the exact quality of the product offered to him.
Often, consumers are offered low-quality products at the price of first-quality products. Our own textile industry is somewhat affected by competing countries where salaries are much lower than in ours.
I hope that the inspectors appointed by the government to enforce compliance with this legislation will make rather frequent checks so that the law is enforced and all producers, mainly those in the Canadian textile industry, are protected as they should be.
March 2, 1970

As regards volunteers, I believe the government has resorted tor too long to its policy of non interference, especially as far as the textile industry is concerned. Today we have to cope with rather acute problems. It is about time for the government to take rigid measures so as to ensure the respect of our own laws on the part of the countries who are exporting their products to this country.
We must realize the importance of the part played by foreign countries on the Canadian market. Allow me to quote a few statistics for 1966. During that year, we received from foreign countries for $19.32 per head of textile products, as against $10.89 in the United Kingdom, $6.07 in the United States and $4.95 in the Common Market countries.
That means that we always resorted in the past to a volunteer policy with regard to the importation of textile products. As for the foreigners who came to Canada to sell their own products, we also let them free to advertise as they pleased. It was about time we had a law like this one with regulations concerning advertising, labelling, analysis and anything that concerns the sale of textile products.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Even if this legislation does not settle the problems now facing the textile industry, I think that in the long run, it will actually bring a valid, though incomplete, solution, and I hope that before long the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) will announce, as he said, a new bill to establish a comprehensive policy regarding the Canadian textile industry, particularly that of Quebec, because over 85,000 workers are drawing their main income from this industry, not to mention some 100,000 workers in the ready-to-wear industry.
I think it is most important to introduce such bills in the House in order to protect our textile industry which is, I think, the third largest in Canada.
Therefore, I hope that before long measures such as this one will be adopted so that our textile industry can hold the rank to which it is entitled in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has introduced this particular bill. Some time ago, back in October, 1968, I myself presented a private member's
Textile Labelling Act
bill which attempted to do in five lines what the minister is attempting to do in 12 pages. But I think that essentially the purposes of the two are the same, and that we will get from this bill correct labelling of fibre content.
Correct labelling is very important, Mr. Speaker, but the trouble is that even correct fibre labelling will not necessarily solve one problem, which happens to be the education of consumers with respect to the properties of all the weird and wonderful names of fibres. So, while this is a step in the right direction, with this particular legislation we are far from being out of the woods.
Like other hon. members who have spoken, it is my hope that this legislation will be followed, either by amendments in committee or perhaps by further legislation, if that is the better way of doing it, which would expand the area of consumer protection. I do not wish to bore the House with long lists of names of fabrics which happen to be quite unintelligible to me, and I am sure as well to other hon. members, and knowing whether or not these fibres are in garments is of no value to the consumer. But this information is of value to the dry cleaners and other persons handling garments in a professional way, because they have the expertise to understand the purposes of this labelling.
But I would mention a couple of areas where we must deal with some problems when this bill is in committee, or else by the introduction of subsequent legislation. The first has already been referred to in this House. It is the question of handling instructions. For example, if you know that a particular garment is half nylon and half wool you might not know how it should be treated when you are washing or dry-cleaning it. The purpose of a further system of labelling would be to indicate the ironing temperature that the housewife should use when ironing the garment. It would indicate the water temperature for both machine washing and hand washing.
I have in mind the system used in Europe and in England whereby through symbols the housewife, and even someone completely uneducated in these matters, such as a bachelor like myself, will know how garments should be treated. I have a Swedish label here which I wish I could table as an example. It gives the wool and artificial fibre content, and the temperature at which the garment should be ironed. It tells you that it should be steam ironed, and it tells you it should be dry

March 2. 1970
Textile Labelling Act
cleaned. It has a little X on it which indicates that it should not be washed.
The shirt I have on, which is an English shirt, has a label on the tail which says, "machine washing-warm-minimum 40 degrees Centigrade; hand washing-warm-40 degrees Centigrade-do not rub-spin-do not hand wring." It also gives the bleaching instructions and the ironing instructions. That is the label on the tail of my shirt, Mr. Speaker, and I can assure you that it is not a Stanfield product.
It is the wrong colour.

Perhaps we could adopt a similar system in Canada, so that when you buy longjohns from the family concern of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), or otherwise, you will know exactly how to treat them to avoid the embarrassing situation of having your longjohns shrink on you. This is something which must be included in future legislation or, as I have suggested, in amendments proposed to this bill in committee. Indeed, it was the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) who suggested that this would be the way of dealing with it. Perhaps the minister, when he comes before the committee, willl be able to explain why he has not done so at this time, and I hope he will be able to satisfy the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and myself.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Now, I wish to refer to one other point which is not mentioned in the bill, but which is a critical matter. It has to do with the flammability of fabrics. Last year in the United States there were approximately 1,500 to 3,000 deaths caused by garments catching fire. We can assume that in Canada the number of deaths per 10,000 population would be higher because of our different climatic conditions. It is extremely important that children's clothing in particular be treated so that they are less flammable than normally. Perhaps this is not so important for natural wool, which has a good resistance to fire, but most of the new fabrics coming out are based on petroleum products or wood products and are highly inflammable. It is important that some system of testing be established so that garments can be tested for flammability and this could be marked on the garment itself.
I do not want to belabour the point but in the Vancouver Sun of November 6, there is

an item headed, "Fire Kills Resident in Sr. Citizens' Home in Nanaimo," and I quote:
A fire department spokesman said the preliminary investigation indicated that the woman's clothing caught fire when she came in contact with a hotplate.
The day following, in the Victoria newspaper under the headline, "Hands, Tummy Scorched Blouse Smoking Mess" there was a description of an accident which took place in a high school in my riding. A girl suffered bums as a result of her blouse catching fire in the cooking class at school when her garment happened to be near a hotplate. This is the sort of thing, especially where children are concerned, that we should be able to do something about with a system of labelling. Perhaps some fabrics should be banned outright if they do not meet certain criteria, particularly artificial fabrics. On some ships such as the Queen Elizabeth II, almost all the furnishings are of wool because of this problem of the flammability of artificial fabrics. Perhaps this problem is not too well publicized in Canada, but perhaps the minister, by legislation or by advertising campaigns, could make people aware of it. In my opinion, this bill should be amended or the minister should bring in another bill similar to the United States act which is 15 USC 1191, 67 Stat. 111. This is the American Flammable Fabrics Act which has the same purpose, that of attempting to reduce danger to the consumer who might innocently buy a garment or fabric with a high flammability level.
Only if we can get a decent system of labelling in this country, with the flammability of materials marked on the garment, will the consumer be able to determine which fabrics are most desirable. This is particularly important in respect of children's garments where the buyer of the garment may not be as concerned about the problem as an adult would be.
With these provisions and reservations, Mr. Speaker, I endorse the bill which the minister's Parliamentary Secretary so ably brought in and presented to us. I hope that in committee some of these other factors will be looked into and that amendments to this particular legislation or future legislation will deal with the points I have raised this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of saying a few brief words on this bill concerning the labelling, sale, importation and advertising of textiles. First of all, however, I want to compliment the Parliamentary Secretary to the
March 2, 1970

Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the able way in which he introduced this legislation. This may be the first time he has introduced legislation and I think it is rather unfortunate that he did not have a better bill to introduce.
My remarks are going to be along the line of asking, why take the time of this House and time of the committee to introduce a 'half way measure bill', an ad hoc piece of legislation which does not give consumers what they want, nor does those things which the textile industry wants? For the life of me, I cannot understand why the government brought in this half way measure. Indeed, I feel like asking the government to withdraw this bill and bring in another that would give the consumer what he wants, namely, labelling to indicate the way in which the material should be cleaned; its safety features; how it should be pressed or ironed, etc. I cannot do better than refer to what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) said when he gave all the reasons why this bill Was ineffective and why it was a half-way measure. I cannot understand why the government did not complete the bill. There are some useful things in the bill, but before I describe those let us take a look at the practical application of it.
Here is a bill asking the industry to make, print or produce labels that will be attached or fastened to the various pieces of fabric. The industry, therefore, as soon as this bill is passed and implemented, has to have labels manufactured or printed. Now, the industry may order a year's supply of labels on which would be printed the percentages of the various fibres, etc. Then, the government may introduce another bill dealing with the aspects of cleaning, safety features and all the other symbols that the consumer wants. This would mean that the industry would have to scrap the original labels and buy new ones. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we could get together on this thing and save the manufacturer some money in the cost and preparation of labels.
These are the practical aspects about which we should be thinking, Mr. Speaker. Let us not deal only with theory. I hope this bill will be studied in detail in committee, and I should like to ask a few questions that may be answered there. The trade finds it difficult to understand this piece of legislation as it nows exists. For instance, the percentage of textile fibre; is it the percentage of textile fibre or is it the percentage of the total weight of the product? And who is going to 21701-58
Textile Labelling Act
pay the fine if a garment is not labelled according to the terms of the legislation? Is it the manufacturer or the person selling it? And if it happens to be an imported article, will the importer have to pay the fine?
I could not help but note that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) was called to order when talking about importation. If we allow the importation of textiles to continue we may not need to worry about a bill to cover labelling; they will all be labelled in the United States or some other part of the world. Then, does the label have to be sewn on the garment or could the manufacturer put the textile product in a polythene bag and put the printing on the bag? Will that suffice? The bill does not spell this out too clearly. If the bill becomes law, I hope manufacturers will be given an opportunity to use up their old labels, before having to purchase new ones.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Of course, the matter of inspection will create tremendous problems and many inspectors will be required. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich spoke about symbols, about the cleaning and washing of fabric, and certainly illustrated his point that great confusion may result in the industry, and among consumers, particularly when generic names are introduced on labels. I submit that the confusion then will be greater even than now. This matter ought to be considered when the bill goes to committee. I realize that the 2,000 odd brand names of manmade fibres created in this great technological age have brought problems to the consumer, who finds it much more difficult to choose now than he did when he had only wool, cotton, linen and silk from which to choose.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I fault this bill for being a half way, ad hoc, incomplete kind of measure which is a waste of the time of the House and of the committee. I am in favour of sending the bill back to the department with the request that they bring in a complete, up to date bill which will give the Consumers' Association what it has asked for and the general public the protection and information they requested.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief.
I simply have a few questions to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Langlois).

March 2. 1970
Textile Labelling Act
I would like to know who actually made this proposal and who will be mostly affected by the bill? I am asking this simply because, as other members, in particular the member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard), I am interested in knowing what effect the bill will have on the textile industry which is facing numerous problems.
It has even been mentioned that an industry in my riding which has 700 or 800 employees might be closed.
I am surely not against the protection of consumers. I think that most consumers have a right to be protected and to know what they are buying and wearing. They are nevertheless interested in those problems, since they are the ones who spend money to buy textile products.
The industry has a great number of employees and this is why I would like to know who is the sponsor of this bill and what will be its effect on the textile industry. The committee will perhaps provide an answer if the parliamentary secretary is unable to do so.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NATIONAL CONFERENCE ON UNIFORM STANDARDS AT PRIMARY AND SECONDARY LEVELS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government of Canada should consider the advisability of taking the initiative in securing the collaboration of the provinces in the convening of a national conference on uniform standards in primary and secondary education.

He said: At the outset, Mr. Speaker, let me make this clear: I do realize that education is a provincial responsibility under our present constitution and I do not believe the federal government should become involved in education to a greater extent than at present. Section 93 of the British North America Act clearly defines the rights of the provinces in the field of education. This situation has resulted, however, in the development of ten educational systems, each claiming to be of superior quality. I believe we have good provincial educational systems, but what concerns me most is that each province in Canada has	determined its	standardindependently	and evaluated	its own
processes.

That is why I introduced the motion we are debating today. The problem of education is important enough indeed to be discussed in the House, especially if we intend to coordinate the ideas and the education programs of the various provinces.
The motion advocates the organization of a national conference to establish uniform standards in all provinces concerning the education of our children.
This means that a student will not be handicapped when, for instance, his parents are forced to move to another province. As stated in the Winter 1968 issue of The Canadian Public Administration, interprovincial cooperation in the field of education has improved over the years.
Officials of various departments have met from time to time, but this co-operation is not quite enough to solve the problems of education on a national scale.
I am interested in this subject because many Canadians move from one province to another in the course of a year.

According to the annual statistical report published by the departmental services offices of the Department of National Health and Welfare covering 1968-69, 53,503 families moved within Canada in that year. On an average there are two children to a family, so more than 100,000 boys and girls moved from one province to another during the past year. I submit that this is a substantial figure and if I were permitted to hazard a guess I would estimate that at least half these students encountered a loss of credits in some way or another as a result of travelling from one province to the next. It is obvious that
March 2, 1970

this would have occurred. I encountered this difficulty myself as a young student attending three universities; each time one goes to a new university one encounters a new system of credits, and some credits are lost because each province looks upon its own system as being the best. Each province is proud of its system of education, and rightly so. As I suggested earlier, the provinces are doing a fairly good job in educating our children, at least in my opinion. We have a good educational system. My concern is that there is insufficient co-ordination or co-operation between the provinces in this field.
Some hon. members might object to the government of Canada taking the initiative in the calling of a national conference on education, which is what this resolution asks. However, no province has seen fit to take the initiative in the past. We know that the premiers meet in Ottawa every now and then, that the ministers of finance are called to Ottawa every so often and that various provincial ministers of other departments come to Ottawa from time to time to discuss matters with their counterparts. So the way is already prepared, as it were, for a national conference on education. There have been some meetings between education ministers in the past, but I do not feel they discussed this particular subject sufficiently or, at least, to my satisfaction. This could certainly be a topic of discussion for once, particularly since we are in the process of drawing up a new constitution, and education is involved in these considerations. Again, I am not suggesting that the source of authority be changed from provincial to federal. Rather, I have in mind that we should co-operate in order to avoid the time of our students being wasted through no fault of their own.
It has been said that home ownership in Ottawa lasts on an average for seven years. This figure may be wrong, but it gives us an idea of the mobility of Canadians. From the fact that 56,000 families moved from one province to another in a single year, it can readily be seen that Canadians are quite mobile. Mobility is the trend today, particularly among young families. They move. They visit other parts of the country. For my part,
I find it shameful that some provinces should not recognize the educational standards of others. I might add that even within a province standards sometimes vary.
I do not wish to speak at length on this motion. I recognize that others wish to say a few words. I know that other hon. members
Conference on Education Uniformity have written theses or papers on this subject; they have told me of their desire to speak on the motion.

As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I do not object to the contents of the courses offered by the provinces. I think that the variety of courses is all the better for Canada. I do not think that the same textbooks should be used throughout Canada or that the same courses in geography or mathematics should be given everywhere. But while taking variety into account, the educational level should be similar and this is what is most important. It is not necessary that in all the provinces, the textbooks and the courses in physics and chemistry or in any other branch be similar, but it is essential that the level be the same, because the particular Characteristics of each province's programs are surely valuable. I know that in certain areas in Canada, there are some courses available which do not interest other provinces, but I think that courses of equal level should be recognized as such throughout Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

The level of education could be set by conducting standardization tests. Various tests are given students today. For example, most of the students entering universities in Canada and the United States are subjected to uniform testing to establish their level of education. I suggest this could also be done not only at the secondary level of education but also at the elementary level, perhaps after grade six, at junior high and, of course, at senior high. This testing could be administered by the school system, and efforts could be co-ordinated with the various provinces. If a standardization test were applied after the primary or elementary level of education all across Canada, it could serve as a guide when families moved from one province to another.
I am not saying that all the various provinces should use the same manual or textbooks, but rather that the students who have taken various courses should be given full credit for them. Most of the time what happens is that the students take what is really a backward step in their education when moving to another province. This is because each province feels, and rightly so, that its education system is better than its neighbours.

Conference on Education Uniformity
I realize that education is a provincial matter. All I am asking for in this motion is for a conference on education to be called by the federal government, particularly at a time when we are debating our constitution, in order to standardize education across Canada in a better fashion than has been the case in the past.
It might be argued that the federal government has no jurisdiction over the matter of education. However, in light of the money that is disbursed by the federal government for educational purposes, one soon realizes that the federal government must concern itself with education, and I think is so concerned. The federal government should work toward establishing standards for school children, which would be of great assistance to those who travel.
As I say, Canada is a young country. Many members of the armed forces are called upon to travel from province to province within the school year. All kinds of people have to travel, young and old. This is why I feel that the matter should be debated, and why I bring it to the floor of the House of Commons. I advocate the holding of a national conference to determine ways and means of providing standards of education for Canadian school children.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the persistent complaints about Canadian education is the lack of uniformity among the ten provincial school systems. This dissatisfaction is mentioned most often by those who speak on behalf of pupils involved in interprovincial transfer. Educational systems and standards do vary from province to province, and students who transfer are likely to find such differences as grade organization, program offerings, course content, matriculation requirements and the opportunity for second language study.
Having said that, like the hon. member opposite I, too, should like to draw attention to the fact that we are on very delicate ground here from the constitutional point of (view. As we are all aware, this is an area highly cherished by the provinces, and which unquestionably under section 93 of the Act does fall within their sphere of responsibility.
The hon. member commented on the holding of a national conference to deal with this matter. I believe that early in his remarks he indicated that the provincial ministers are very well aware of the problems raised in his motion, that they have taken steps over the

past four years to grapple with these problems.
In 1967 there was established a standing council of provincial ministers of education with a permanent secretariat. Under their aegis various meetings have been convened, bringing together representatives of the various provincial departments to consider mutual problems and to try and resolve them.
What is meant by uniform standards? I assume that the hon. member is asking for uniform standards in curriculum at grade level. If he is, then I suggest his thoughts are running contrary to present thoughts on education. The whole question of uniformity and standardization in education is a particularly current topic in view of the increasing emphasis being given by reformers in the educational system on the needs of the individual student.
The Hall-Denis report "Living and Learning", recently published in Ontario, is symptomatic of this trend. If I may quote from the report:
The curriculum must provide a greater array of! learning experiences than heretofore. Classes must be more mobile, within and beyond the local environment, and the rigid position of education must yield to a flexibility capable of meeting new needs.
And again:
Our schools often expect the child ... to be stuffed or programmed like a computer ... Recently, however, there has been in many schools a transition from this outdated approach toward a child-centred program in which every effort is made to fit the learning opportunity to the potential, tempo, and level of understanding of the individual child.
.. .the ultimate responsibility for making decisions concerning pupils belongs to the teacher, who must have the competence and authority to do so. Principals and their staffs need relative autonomy in matters of curriculum planning.
These are but a few of the progressive, liberal concepts of education presently being advocated. It is clear that the very notions of uniformity and standardization represent an anathema to the reform-minded educator. Basically the system is trying to promote innovation, flexibility, greater teacher freedom in the curriculum, and more local responsibility. I think that all who are involved in education view this as a trend that they consider desirable and which they are most anxious to encourage.
In past years, ministers of education of the four western provinces had close co-operation on these matters, and it was relatively easy for them to establish some inter-provincial guidelines when schools were functioning by
