grade promotion and relatively rigidly structured programs. However, over the last two or three years, with the new trends in education based on the thoughts to which I have referred, they have found it much more difficult to make arrangements to cope with today's demands.
This is not to suggest that children of families that move from province to province do not face educational problems. However, I should like to say that I do not think that those problems are as great or grave, from the numerical point of view, as the hon. member has indicated. As he pointed out, a great many of these transfers are made during the summer months when disruption was much less than it would be during the school year.

It seems to me the central question is not a constitutional one. I think it is quite proper,
4246	COMMONS
Conference on Education Uniformity as the resolution is worded, for the federal government within the general peace, order and good government clause of the constitution to initiate conferences with the provinces on this subject and to propose that the question of uniform standards be addressed and considered. I do not think there is a serious constitutional argument against that.
The real question seems to me to involve the desire to have uniform standards of education. It was not long ago that I think most enlightened opinion in Canada, indeed in the western industrialized world, was to the effect that it was desirable in a state to have common standards throughout so the people could progress according to their age through the educational system, no matter where they happened to live in the country under consideration.
It has been recognized for a number of years by individuals, and more recently by some of the provincial governments within Canada, that uniformity is not a very desirable thing to stress in education. Indeed, it is a very bad thing to stress when we are seriously concerned with the development of creative and responsible human beings. Human beings are not identical in ability, talent or interests. So that the kind of educational system we should have in Canada, or anywhere else as far as that is concerned, is one which would maximize the state's efforts to bring out what is unique in every individual and maximize the efforts of our teaching institutions to be flexible in their approach to children rather than to impose a rigid structure on whole groups simply because they are at the same chronological age level.
Therefore, the argument that was offered by the member for Southwestern Nova (Mr. Comeau) for uniformity as a desirable objective, is not a good one in principle, and seems therefore, to be unacceptable. He said that our educational system should not concentrate so much on uniformity within our federal state, or even uniformity within our provinces, but rather on breaking down the rigid patterns and approaching each child as much as possible in terms of the allocation of resources and treating him as a unique human being. It is not even necessary to keep to a strict grade system.
If it were argued that what we should have are relatively frequent national conferences on education at which all the provinces come together to discuss education at the elementary and secondary school levels, then I, for one, would be in favour of this kind of development. However, what they should be discussing is not the imposition of a uniform standard from one coast to the other but what each province is doing; what is new in Nova Scotia; what is new in British Columbia, and what interesting pedagogical techniques are being introduced here or there. They should be discussing what new courses are being introduced, for example, in Alberta, that should now be introduced in Ontario. It seems to me that a conference organized on a national basis under the auspices of the federal government which seeks to bring responsible people from the provinces together to discuss this matter could indeed be very useful. speechtext:
First of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) for introducing the very important subject contained in the resolution for our consideration. It seems to me that our educational system has always been one of the most serious matters in the whole realm of public affairs. Already in this session I expressed in the debate on the constitution my view that one of the sacred cows in our constitution, and our whole political philosophy, is the belief that education must be controlled completely by the provinces. I am of the opinion that the complex educational structure which we have in this country is not either sufficient or adequate to meet the needs of modern Canada. It might have been adequate and sufficient in a previous age when people in this country lived in one province, or indeed in one place in a province, for practically all their lives, but it is not suitable for the kind of mobile population we now have.
It can be taken for granted that many, if not most, people in this country will make one or more major moves during the course of their adult lives, taking their children with them from one part of the country to another. These moves are important to our citizens in terms of the advancement of their careers and the development of their capacity in whatever line of activity they are following. They should also be important not only for the adults but for the children, because the mobility that we have in this country gives us an opportunity to show our people and our children all parts of Canada. However, far too often the result of one of these major moves of the family is not to enhance the education and broaden the horizons of the children but to confront them with grave, if not insoluble problems.
I favour conferences on education. I am not so sure that we should strive to have a lockstep, uniform curriculum in Canada, but I doubt very much if that was really in the mind of the sponsor of this motion. He is shaking his head, so I can tell that it was not. He is concerned I think, as I am, with the children who are confronted daily with the result of the present absurd educational system which we have in Canada. I was shocked to hear the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) ask: "What does it matter if a child loses one tenth, one
DEBATES	4247

I find this kind of thinking hard to understand, especially when it comes from a person with the kind of child oriented type of philosophy which is dominant in Ontario at present. This is what this discussion is all about. It is about the effect of this absurd system of education, not on parents, educators or teachers, but on children. The results are frequently serious and sometimes catastrophic.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first of all want to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) on two aspects of his remarks; first, his sincerity, and second, I believe he has put his finger on the essence of the problem, and that is the Canadian educational system as it affects the children. Therein is the only area of discussion.
I think that the motion introduced by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) has really two aspects to it. The first aspect is that of the federal government taking some initiative in the field of education, which in itself could touch off a lengthy and worthwhile debate. The second aspect is the specific question of the convening of a conference to try and establish some general, broad areas of agreement among the provinces, or at least some uniformity up to a point in the field of education.
I listened to the hon. member for London West (Mr. Buchanan) and to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). I was a little bit disappointed because I think what both hon. members did was to define the motion as it is before us in order to justify what is a very popular stand. It is very popular today for educators to talk about freedom
March 2, 1970	COMMONS
of choice, the freedom of choice of the student with respect to the curriculum, so that in the classroom students may progress at an individual rate. This has been very popular for the last decade and there is no argument there. But it all depends on how you define uniform standards.
In the few minutes we have listened to this debate it has been obvious that there is a great dilemma between those people who advocate a certain uniform standard across the nation and those people who argue that there should be completely individual instruction, that there should not be uniformity provincially or even at the community level. The consideration of the individual should extend to the classroom level, where the curriculum is to be a very specific thing and is to exist for the child alone. Somewhere between those two extremes lies a meaningful approach to the problem of education in Canada.
I do not think anyone will disagree that there is no way a nation can lay down uniform standards for what actually will take place in an individual classroom. I do not think the hon. member for South Western Nova even suggested or even thought that would be a desirable aim of the Canadian educational system. Certainly, the classroom curriculum, the actual teaching in the classroom, has to be geared to the individual. The five foot high-jump concept in education has to go. The classroom curriculum has to be geared to each individual considering his unique environment, his unique hereditary background, and the summation of the qualities making up his individualism. All this demands that he be given an individual curriculum, but certainly this is not the intent of the motion. The intent of the motion, as I see it, it to give some credence to the widely accepted belief that across the Canadian nation, just as in the United States, there is a need for laying down some uniform standards.
Here I speak of uniformity of standards with respect to general philosophy or general principles, which will ease the tremendous burden borne by thousands of families who have become mobile as a result of the developed society in which we are living, as compared with the society of our grandfather's day. I can really sympathize with the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton when I realize the kind of constituency he has. Even in the town of Gander, which has a population of only 9,000 people, we experience a tremendous movement of people. Every year
DEBATES	4249
Conference on Education Uniformity between 100 and 150 new families move into the town. They come from a wide variety of backgrounds, and in such a circumstance there is a need for uniform educational standards. But again, it really depends on how you define "curriculum". The professional experts in Canada define curriculum in a very broad sense-what are your goals, objectives and aims, and all of these components are taken into consideration when deciding the curriculum.
If you look across Canada today you see we have ten different approaches to the curriculum question. If you study the underlying philosophy, aims and objectives of each individual province with respect to education you will find that they are all different. British Columbia, for instance, places a great deal of emphasis on streaming. What we traditionally used to call grade 8 is now called level 8, because the teachers have not found another name for "grade" which is an unpopular term. When pupils reach level 8, they move out into various streams and eventually each stream leads to a particular objective orientated toward university on the one hand or trade on the other.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Other provinces, and I can think of Alberta, place much more emphasis on a general approach to education; they emphasize the general rather than the specific. Other provinces believe that until the student reaches the end of secondary school he should not be involved in anything that could be classified as a specific job or occupational orientation. In other words, up to grade 12 we speak only of general education; that is the basic aim and it is a very general foundational kind of approach. Still other provinces have greatly emphasized religious training. I can think of a province which emphasizes the denominational system of education almost to the detriment of other aspects of the total development of the child. We can take Quebec and Newfoundland as examples.
In Canada we can come to terms on the general, underlying philosophy of education, and that is what actually happens in the classroom. We can, therefore, have some standardization of approach. Certainly the hon. member for South Western Nova never meant to leave the impression, nor did he say, that the conference he referred to in his motion should specify what type of textbooks should be used in a particular grade level or what marks should be expected in an examination or any such standardized procedures. I
4250	COMMONS DEBATES	March 2. 1970
Conference on Education Uniformity think a number of hon. members, and one in particular, has gone out of his way to shift the emphasis of the resolution to suit his own purpose, and perhaps he has clouded the issue.
I support this kind of resolution because I am aware of the extent of the mobility of our population in Canada today, and it will become increasingly mobile. Since I have had a family I have been in 13 different environments, from the extreme west coast to the extreme east coast and in between. I am not, however, nearly as mobile-prone as some public servants and members of the armed services.
In Newfoundland, for example, 10,000 people leave the province every year. We just have grade 11 there, no grade 12, so when students arrive in Ontario the problem is how they are going to identify with grade 12. Do you take a grade 10 student and make him grade 11? They have found, for example, that in many cases grade 10 standards are equivalent to grade 11 because of the more diversified approach to the four years of secondary school in Ontario. Ours is a more academic approach, and consequently our students are as capable at the end of grade 10 as is the average Ontario student at the end of grade 11. You can believe that, it is not one for Ripley's.
What I am trying to say, Mr. Speaker, is that the converse is also true. In Nova Scotia, for example, you need grade 12 to get into university but in Newfoundland you only need Grade 11, so a special provision has been made to allow our grade 11 students to enter first year university in Nova Scotia. If they are smart and bright enough, they can overcome the slight deficiency in the academic background, but at least they are accepted. However, I am sure Nova Scotia is not going to continue this approach.
There are many areas of standardization in the field of education, Mr. Speaker, such as reading, mathematics, university expectations qualifications and the general broad principles of education, which could be accepted across the whole Canadian nation. I should like to go one step further than the hon. member for South Western Nova and suggest that it is time the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland-in fact all the provinces of Canada and the federal government-get off their high horses as to the constitutional rights regarding education. Let us face the fact that education today, the development of human resources, is a most important area in which the government should be involved.

Let us start talking about the individual, the development of the youngster and try to set some national goals and expectations and perhaps aim at the establishment of a national ministry of education one day.
Right now the federal government is going through the back door. It is involved in education through about 17 different government departments. At the same time, if a question is asked in this House about education of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or anybody else, the answer is that it is a provincial responsibility. I think this is a good resolution and I should like to see other members introduce other resolutions in order to open up the area of education for discussion, and for some specific action.

Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me necessary to have a discussion of this nature in light of the announcement made by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) responsible for the Wheat Board-a statement that was supported and concurred in by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson)-which could very well indicate that there is to be a new departure for farming in western Canada and which certainly indicates that there are to be marked and radical changes in the pattern of farming in that part of the country.
When someone in authority suggests that it is advisable to take 22 million acres of land
Wheat Acreage Reduction out of wheat production in one year in western Canada, and when you consider that last year the total acreage seeded for wheat was 24.5 million acres, I think one can grasp the concept and sweep of this proposed policy. I do not know what would be said if someone were to suggest a similar policy for the steel industry of Ontario, for the automobile industry of Ontario or for the corn growing industry of Ontario. Of course, industries in other provinces could serve as examples. Certainly you would know that there was to be a major disruption in the industrial heartland of Canada if such announcements were made.
When we discuss these kinds of changes in wheat farming, we are talking about the basis of the farming economy in western Canada because we are talking about the agricultural heartland of western Canada. Let us make no mistake; let us be under no illusion: that is what we are talking about. That farming economy has as its base the production of cereal crops. No matter whether farmers are producing beef or hogs-and these remarks apply to all but the small proportion of farmers who are in ranching-cereals are used in the entire feeder operation.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
If the proposal is successful to its ultimate degree and the proposed number of acres are taken out of production, I shall be profoundly disturbed and dismayed because, Mr. Speaker, if we succeed in taking so many acres out of wheat production, and experience a crop year in Saskatchewan or western Canada generally like the one of 1961, we will all face nothing less than a major disaster.
That little wheat plant may not stand very tall, but the by-products of the wheat plant, together with barley and oats, provide much of the roughage for the beef cattle kept in western Canada. This House must be made aware of the vast shifts in production that can take place within that region. In 1961 we harvested 260 million bushels of wheat in western Canada and in 1968 we harvested 807 million bushels. That is a vast difference. If you look through the figures in the Wheat Board report you will note that we had a comparatively high production in the period 1964 to 1968. In the last four years we have harvested exceptionally large crops. This is in part responsible for the large carryover which we now have. Also responsible is the failure of our marketing policies to keep pace with production.
4252	COMMONS
Wheat Acreage Reduction
In this respect the government and those responsible are justified in being concerned about the continual build-up of stocks and the fact that the stocks have not been moving. If they had said to the western farmers that over the next two, three or four years there would be a gradual program of adjustment, possibly it would have been considered, although the marketing factor would still require top priority. This is not what they did; they talked of this reduction in one year and they are using two means to achieve it. The farmer is being offered $6 an acre if he takes his land out of wheat, or $10 an acre if he will plant forage crops. But there is the catch. Behind the carrot is a stick. It is a pretty big stick that goes along with that carrot. The farmer is being told: If you do not reduce your acreage, if you do not get in line with government policy and wisdom and with the savvy and know-how that exists in the halls of the experts in Ottawa, you will not be able to deliver over and above a certain amount of wheat.
I will not go into the technicalities and the particular acreages involved. In a general way, the farmer was told that if he had so many acres in summer fallow last year, he could deliver wheat on 25 per cent of it: that, plus what he put in summer fallow this year, plus his forage crop acreage, would be his delivery quota. This is the stick: if he does not go along with government policy, he will have a backlog of wheat which he will not be able to deliver.
This plan inevitably envisages a tremendous increase in summer fallow in western Canada. It carries within it the risk of severe soil erosion and damage in the Prairie region, not only wind erosion but water erosion. There is a proposal that as of July 15 farmers can sow some cover crops, but anyone who has farmed as long as I have in Saskatchewan knows that if you have any alternative you do not leave summer fallow bare until July 15. If you do, you have rocks in your head.
These are the faults I find with this program, Mr. Speaker. It does not take into account the necessary protection of our resources it does not take into account the protection of the farmers. In one swipe it knocks out the privileges of the unit delivery quota of the small farmer. This quota is important and is needed by the small farmer; however, it is to be his no longer.
There is talk of what is to be done with our marketing program. The effectiveness of our marketing has not been good. There is not

enough said in these proposals about what is going to be done to correct that situation. The Economic Council urges action to increase Canada's wheat sales. A recent report states:
Mr. Hudson studied the competitive position of Canadian Wheat in 23 selected wheat markets, and says there is a variety of reasons for the deterioration of Canada's share.
These include lack of uniformity in the protein content of Canadian wheat shipments, a lack of flexibility in pricing, insuflieient market development work-
This is a severe condemnation of what has been done in the way of marketing Canada's wheat in the last few years. I could go back to the minutes which I have. When the Minister without Portfolio in charge of the Wheat Board was in London he had meetings, following which there was a statement in the press that buyers in London said protein grading in our wheat was not up to the standard of other wheat they were buying.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief time I have left I want to point out some other effects of this policy. Australia increased its sales up to December by 32.9 million bushels, Argentina by 1.4 million bushels and the United States by 12 million bushels. Our sales dropped by 37.4 million bushels. These are the figures: they tell the story of the western farmer.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I note the statement of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board in this respect. He believes that as a result of the proposed tremendous reduction in acreage he will be able to approach the other wheat producers and that they will fall in with this pattern. This is nonsense. It may be some countries will do so. I do not know what the United States will do. They are cheering us on, but why not? I am always willing to cheer the little guy on when he is fighting-he may even win-as long as the blows do not come my way. But do hon. members suppose that the U.S.S.R. will reduce its wheat production? They would be insane if they did. This is an example of nineteenth century economics being applied to Canada in the year 1970. It is laissez-faire economics, as out of date today as the horse and buggy.
Some people imagine that we shall be able to persuade other countries to reduce wheat acreage to a corresponding extent. But the western wheat grower will be the No. 1. mark in such a deal. He will pay the shot. It is time realistic policies were followed. We can accept a gradual reduction over a number of
DEBATES	4253
Wheat Acreage Reduction years if that is necessary, but before we are asked to accept a reduction of the size proposed we want to know what producers in other countries intend to do. Nothing can be gained from speculating, and that is all we are doing now. We cannot dump the whole burden on the shoulders of the farmers. Certainly the Canadian taxpayer is ready to put some money into this plan, but a far heavier price will be paid by the farmers.
I would be pleased if the minister could assure us that he had received commitments from the U.S.S.R., France, Argentina, Australia and the other great wheat producers to lower their acreages. But in that case, Mr. Speaker, there would be no need to consider a reduction of 22 million acres: it would not take a reduction of that size to bring world supplies into balance, if that is our objective.
It seems to me the sole objective should be the need to provide food for the people of the world who do not have it, something which has not been considered at all in this program. For these reasons I urge the government to reconsider its views and modify certain aspects of this program before it is too late and before too much damage is done. No one knows what the result will be in 1971 when Canadians will be literally reaping the harvest of what hon. members opposite did in 1970.

Mr. Speaker, will you give the dog a bone? We have a justifiable reason for complaining when we are told to cut off our production. Has the government ever told the people of Quebec who produced 80 million of the 90 million pounds of surplus butter to cut off production? There has been talk of a reduction of 10 million acres, but you must still consider the 150 million surplus.
I know the people who live in the constituency of the hon. member for Bruce. I was in his constituency. Let me say to the world, to all Canadians and all Members of Parliament: We would like the opportunity to buy a tractor, which would not cost $20,000-as suggested by the Prime Minister-but $6,000 if we were allowed to purchase those manufactured by Japan, Czechoslovakia, Russia and other countries. Perhaps we could afford to buy one even with a dollar a bushel for our wheat. I do not know but, by God, I think we could try.
You tell us on the one hand to cut down on Che production of food, and on the other hand to get out and produce. I think you must admit that something is wrong. I have had the opportunity of travelling far enough in this world to find out that some people struggle in the rice paddies and in the mud in India in order to eke out a living. If these people have to wallow in the mud there has to be some-

Wheat Acreage Reduction thing wrong in our thinking. We should have tractors to do that work rather than men struggling with bullocks and everything else in 120 degree temperatures. Somewhere along the line we have to work out new ideas.
Perhaps you think in my disgust I am asking too much. Do you expect me to wait for the United States to take over these markets? Do you expect me to wait for the French to take over the markets? This is what they are doing. Japan is ready, and Britain has committed itself. Is this the policy the government is going to follow? This government told the potash industry to cut down 40 per cent on its production, but it tells the farmers to cut down 100 per cent. The government is telling, not only the farmers but other business men they have not a chance, *they are finished. If we follow that stupid dictate the government has given the farmers, impossible as it may seem, the farmers have no choice but to diversify.
I had to break up my operations into three branches-the one-third summer fallow I had last year, one-third in crop I might have put in, and the other in the summer fallow I would have this year anyhow. I say to the government I am going to take its money this summer for the crop I might have put in, and I am going to put it in anyway. I have a few cattle on my place. When I said the other day in the House that all the consultations were based on what the Wheat Board could do, and that too many laws are passed in this House with no idea as to what is the proper way of administering them, I meant it because I as a farmer will be the one who is sacrificed at the altar. The government never consulted anyone and they have never given the Agriculture Committee the opportunity to do so.
I know that some members of the committee, such as the hon. member for Bruce, speak sincerely sometimes, and that the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Lind) speaks hon-

I wish some hon. members here had an opportunity to talk to the people who have to make that decision. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that many farmers decided last year, without the assistance of the government, to reduce their production by 15 per cent. No incentive was given them by the government. They know themselves what they will have to do. But I do not know what will happen next year. I do know that in 1961 I had no crop at all and in 1963 I had trouble with rust, flood and so on, and there was only one good crop year in six years. Does the government think I will take a chance not to put in a crop the one year which might prove to be successful?
What drives me from accepting the government's incentive is the fact that I cannot depend on this government to pull me through during periods when I am up against difficulty. So far they have in desperation come up with some sort of plan. All I can say is, thank God they have come out of their shell because at least from here on we know what they are thinking. They are telling us to get out of business.
An interesting riddle was told me the other day. What is the quickest way of creating a desert out of some of the richest land in the world? The answer is, a Liberal government program. I would have enjoyed the humour except that I myself was involved. I like to think that I can contribute something by paying my taxes. I like to think that we can produce enough food on our farms not only for ourselves but for the rest of the world. It is surprising for the government, in this day and age when a population explosion is taking place and we see on television programs about there being too many people in the world, to be so bankrupt of ideas that it has to tell us to stop growing wheat. There are 188,000 farmers in Canada and they are blamed for causing the ills of this world of millions and millions of people. You have to stretch a country mile to make me believe

that, because we have done our share in feeding the hungry.
As I have pointed out, the government is trying to sacrifice the farmers. Perhaps we should sacrifice the machinery industry, which is not Canadian anyway. Which is better? Perhaps the government is sacrificing the wrong people. I say to the government, and particularly to the minister form Saskatchewan, that I think he has made a valiant effort to redeem himself and his government but he is not fooling me because the summer fallow will create the same problems that we had before. Anybody who knows something about the patterns of summer fallow will understand me and realize that this is not a solution to our problems. Perhaps it is a temporary stopgap and it may bring some relief to the farmers and get a few members to Liberal political meetings out in the west, but so far as the western farmer is concerned the government is a long way away from coming to a solution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the motion before us, not because I am directly interested in the program announced by the minister but because his suggestions to the western provinces resemble all too much what we have had to put up with in other spheres in the eastern provinces. I feel for all the western wheat producers and I understand their anger on hearing about such a program.
I feel that is the best program ever put forward by a Liberal minister and I say it proves what the Liberals are capable of. During the war, the Liberal party paid people to burn goods while today, they are getting ready to pay the producer to stop producing. With programs like that you can imagine where Canada is heading for.
I was reading today in Le Soleil for March 2, about that wonderful program. I was absolutely astounded. This evening, I must bow to the evidence.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
One can read in Le Soleil the minister's statement to the effect that the government of Canada is suggesting that the wheat acreage of 24.5 million acres be reduced by 22 million acres in western Canada. Mr. Speaker, I am just speaking as a humanitarian and I cannot imagine that we have reached the point where we are going to refuse to seed 22 million acres of land to wheat especially when two-thirds of mankind are not eating three
March 2, 1970

meals a day yet. I do not wish any hardship on Canada; however, I am very much afraid that some day it will dearly pay for the lack of action of its leaders.
If the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) as well as the other ministers concerned, namely the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) had done their job instead of travelling as tourists around the world like playboys, today the situation would be quite different. They have taken trips instead of trying to dispose of our dairy products and our wheat. We have a playboy government and we are going to pay for it. The same article, says, and I quote:
Under the law, 5,200 hungry Metis are forbidden to use the wheat given to them by farmers.
This is the case in Meadow Lake which I visited last summer. There I met poor farmers who could have used the wheat which was rotting in the fields. When I saw the sheaves of wheat, I could not believe my eyes. I went quite near to make sure that it was really true. The Metis told me: We cannot even get some to feed our families. Is there anything more shameful than that, Mr. Speaker?
They are not even able to change our financial system so that the production may reach at least the inhabitants of this country. That is shocking to say the least. Instead of adjusting our financial system to production, they are still trying to reduce the latter to the proportion of our financial system. There lies the great evil, Mr. Speaker.
The ministers, who cringe before high finance, will not face facts. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), who worked with us in the past, knows the nature of the problem. But he is swallowed up in that crowd and does not see anything except that this divine financial system must be protected. According to the government, there is no way of modernising our financial system.
I took the floor tonight so that everybody will know about the shameful solution put forward by the government. We are told the implementation of that program, which will be in force for a year, will cost about $100 million to the taxpayers and will affect some 188,000 wheat producers who deliver their products to the Canadian Wheat Board, a government agency that acts as an outlet for wheat, oats and barley sown in the Prairie provinces as well as in some areas of British Columbia. So $100 million will be spent out of the taxpayers' money.
Wheat Acreage Reduction
I wish to draw the attention of the House to the fact that, the people of Quebec will also have to bear the cost of the proposed subsidy intended to discourage the western producers from producing. They are paid not to produce whereas in the East, the idea is to "strangle" the farmers to compel them to abandon their land. Here is now an excerpt from The Star and I quote:
The government will pay $6 per acre up to a maximum ol $6,000 to the farmers-
-who will have the guts to leave their land idle. And those who sow anything but wheat will get $10 per acre up to $10,000.
The department does not even realize the absurdity of the situation. Actually, it has always been more or less unaware of where it was going.
They are doing the same thing in Quebec where they say to the farmers: "Forget all about dairying and start producing meat, and hay." It is the same story in the West, to the extent that within two or three years, our surpluses will be just as high as those we have today with wheat and dairy products.
There is nothing wrong, do we say, in trying to destroy the production granted by Providence to Canada. What we should do is not burn and destroy but go on producing and take whatever steps to bring this production to the hungry.
I believe that out of the 264 members of the House we could manage a sufficient quorum to organize a rund table if the government would only agree sometimes to consult the opposition in order to set up a program of distribution, to feed at least the people in our own country and also the people abroad, thus enabling our farmers to market their production.
But far from it, the government, by means of what they dare call a program, will pay the farmers not to produce.
As I said, I believe this program to be the worst that a minister has ever dared to present to the House for a number of years. Whose fault is it? It is the fault of the ministers who have not done their job.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board did not perform their task. This is why we are not able to sell our present surpluses.
If we gave $100 million to the farmers in order to help them, at least, to sell their wheat at 25 or 50 per cent of its price to the
March 2, 1970

Wheat Acreage Reduction people of Saskatchewan who are "crying" to get some, these $100 million would at least serve some purpose and would not be destructive.
I suggest merely that these $100 million be used to sell wheat at a discount in order to guarantee the western farmers a reasonable price.

Kon. Oito E. Lang (Minister without Portfolio): Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to have this opportunity to speak about the wheat reduction program which was announced in the House last Friday. I am particularly glad to have this opportunity to talk to my colleagues in this House and to hon. members, and perhaps particularly to address myself to hon. members from the provinces or the area of the Wheat Board designated region to which the program particularly applies. It is, Mr. Speaker, of fundamental importance that the farmers of the designated region work together to examine their problems realistically and hard-headedly, and to solve them together with such help as the government of Canada can give them. In developing this program we have been acting on part of a long-term examination of every aspect of the agricultural or grains industry in western Canada.

We were faced with specific decisions about the crop in 1970. Work is going on upon every other facet of the industry because of the difficulties which the industry has faced. speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, what is also completely obvious-it is as clear to the farmers to whom I spoke as it is to me-is that we must be realistic in deciding a number of things, including our best sales prospects. We must be realistic, too, in deciding about our inventory. Not many industries can survive without paying any attention at all to the inventory question, because inventory is expensive. It is expensive to produce and it is expensive to tie up money, even the marginal cost of production, if the inventory is in excess of what is commercially required for sales.
What is also obvious to all of us, surely, is that having determined what is approximately the right inventory, we must over a long period of time keep our production and sales in balance. That is what is at the heart of this problem and this program at this time. An inventory is expensive, not only because of the marginal cost in producing it and the interest lost on that money, not only because of the cost of storage which year after year must be paid while the inventory is carried, but because of the effect it can have on the price of the product in the world when you have excess inventory.
It is important for one other extremely basic reason, and that is because the excessive inventory of wheat in the Prairie region this year was going to have one very clear effect-it was going to press farmers into production of every other crop you can name, so that the excess inventory or surplus problem would have been spread throughout the whole grain industry. Farmers were aware of this fact; they were aware that inventory was in excess.
Generally speaking, they agreed that we are carrying almost one billion bushels of wheat, as we will on July 31 next; we are carrying 500 million bushels more than we

March 2, 1970	COMMONS
ought to for any commercial reason or for any other reason. What we are saying is that if we did not have that extra amount, on all analysis of how long we would have to carry even the upper bushels of the rest that we have, we would be carrying it a very long time before we had an opportunity to move it.
That means we would have enough without the 500 million bushels to meet all prospective sales opportunities and anything else in the way of aid or anything else we might do with it. Even in aid, the world can take only so much. When you start with a bushel of wheat and put it into an edible form like bread, the wheat in the bread comprises perhaps only about one-fifth of the cost. You need money to move it and you need money to mill it; you need to build ports and roads and trucks for the countries where the wheat is to be taken.
The simple proposition was, Mr. Speaker, that this inventory was lying as a great burden upon the farm industry, a burden costing millions of dollars a year to carry, and was causing distortion in every direction in regard to crops. I said we must maximize our sales.

I was sure, Mr. Speaker, that was his basic intent but it was rather unfortunate that he pointed his finger at the Wheat Board in attempting to do it.
Sales have lagged in the first half of this crop year, but by the end of the crop year exports will amount to 375 million bushels, which is higher than all years but one between 1943, when the Wheat Board started, and 1963 when the first sale to Russia was made.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext: This is 1970.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Had this year stood alone in terms of sales, one might have asked: Where is the cash problem about which we have heard to much? But, of course, this year does not stand alone; it stands after two years of very difficult times in terms of sales, and therefore a very difficult cash position for the agricultural community. That is why we have to be concerned. That is why the inventory adjustment, which it was quite logical and clear that this industry had to make, could not be expected to be made by it alone. That is why we had to try to devise a program which faced up to this inventory issue and to the cash problem at the same time. These two things we have put together in an attempt to accomplish the result in as short a time as possible.
Mr. Speaker, the extra 500 million bushels of wheat which are above commercial requirements are expensive to carry. The longer you carry any part of it, the longer you carry that part of the expense. Accordingly, it was clear that what we needed in our attempt to bring this inventory into proper line, and also to avoid the creation of unnecessary and undue surpluses in other crops, was the quickest possible retirement from production of 22 million acres for one year. We looked at the possibilities of doing that over a longer period of time or over a shorter period. Any lengthening of the time simply prolonged the pain and the period in which those acres would have gone into other crops. Hon. members who are farmers know very well that is what would have happened. So we looked at the possibility of doing it in
March 2. 1970

Wheat Acreage Reduction one year and we proposed, with the co-operation of the farmers, that we should try.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
It was also clear that any farmer who had enough wheat on hand to meet all the quota he could expect this year, and also all of the quota which might be available for him in 1970-71, had his gross income established and whether he grew or did not grow more would not affect his gross income in that period. Indeed, to not produce could only conceivably lower his costs and improve his actual cash position while his inventory was being disposed of. In other words, it could temporarily improve his cash position. Accordingly, we have devised a program which has invited him to take 22 million acres out of production this year, to put that land either into summer fallow or some form of minimum maintenance and to put up to 2 million acres of it into forage or grass. We propose to pay him $6 per acre for the additional minimum maintenance acres which the farmer had on his farm, as compared with the previous year, and we propose to pay him an extra $4 an acre for land that was put into grass and stayed there during the following year.
This represents a very important opportunity for the farmers together to reduce their inventory and for the Prairie region, particularly the grains region which has been hardest hit by the cash problem, to obtain a very valuable infusion of cash. The ideal would be for the farmers to take 22 million acres out of wheat and put it into minimum maintenance and forage because, on the best estimates we have available, it is indicated that the acreage which was in non-wheat crops last year is about the right acreage to have in these crops again this year. There may be some switching around of crops; some farmers may move some acres from barley into rapeseed, but the total is about right.
The only way, therefore, we can obtain that result is through the removal from production of the 22 million acres of wheat which are not required to meet any markets in wheat and are not required for any other crops either. This, therefore, represents an opportunity to hon. members to join with us in explaining this program to farmers from one end of the designated region to the other. I ask them to join in a task which represents a challenge for us and for the provincial governments to try to give the very best possible advice to farmers about the form of minimum maintenance which is most desirable in each region.


We recognized that that challenge must be met in the time available but we did not feel it was proper to take more time and lose a whole year in implementing a program of this sort. We were particularly afraid of the impact in other grains which would have occurred in the process.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the minister now answer my question?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for over a year western opposition members have been trying to persuade the government to give some form of assistance to western agriculture to relieve the serious cash position of the farmers due to their inablity to market their grain through the Wheat Board. Last Friday the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) announced that something would be done in this regard. His announcement is apparently supposed to hold the surplus at its present level and at the same time provide the western agriculturist with his living expenses for this crop year. The minister may be a good professor, but he is an awfully poor mathematician. The cash advance will take up at least half the quota that the farmer is going to receive between now and the end of the crop year. The $6 requirement for summer fallow will not pay the cost of summer fallowing. That leaves exactly nothing for the farmer to live on.
The minister says the farmers are prepared to face reality. He said he talked to farmers in Saskatchewan. The only reason they are facing reality is they know this is all the government is going to offer them. There is no point in not facing reality because that is it as far as the government is prepared to go.
The minister went into quite a bit of detail in his announcement dealing with the acreage
4264	COMMONS
Wheat Acreage Reduction reduction. It was interesting to note that the Secretary of Agriculture of the United States lauded the program.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 GRAIN WHEAT-EFFECT OF ACREAGE REDUCTION PROGRAM ON FARMERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks, why not? In answer to a question I asked this afternoon, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) said that the United States was also reducing its acreage. Over the years they have been doing this on a small percentage basis. The fact remains they are still going to grow 45 million acres of wheat. Their gradual reduction seems to make more sense than this crash program which will leave the farmer without any wheat to grow or any crop to change to, because the minister has already intimated that the surplus of other grains is high enough.
Canada is in the position of making a unilateral reduction in a very large acreage of wheat. I am sure this will bring pressure on other governments from the farmers and producers of their countries to maintain production, if not to increase it, because Canada has told the world it is not going to worry about supplying wheat in the export market. We are not going to grow any wheat this year, therefore the other producers are bound to step into what might be called the vacuum.
The minister now says he is going to discuss acreage reduction with other governments. He has evidently forgotten the old adage about locking the barn door after the horse has been stolen. He has given away all his bargaining powers as far as wheat acreage reduction is concerned. He has left it up to our competitors as to whether they will reduce their wheat acreage. My guess is that if they do reduce their wheat acreage, which is doubtful, it will be only a very small amount.
Had the minister made this suggestion last year when opposition members were pressing for payments on a crop reduction basis, any action taken would not have been nearly so drastic. It would have afforded the farmers more room to manoeuvre in crop selection. It would also have benefited those farmers who voluntarily reduced their wheat acreage by five million acres, many of whom will receive little compensation from the scheme this year.
Actually, the minister's statement shows a defeatist attitude on the part of this government which has failed to maintain Canada's share of the export market. It is a cover-up by the government for its failure to do the

DEBATES	March 2, 1970
things necessary to keep our grain economy competitive in world trade. It is a grandiose scheme which will fall far short of its objective to relieve the desperate cash position of the Prairie farmer. The minister knows as well as I that his boast of a $140 million payment is just so much window-dressing simply because it is predicated on the fact that no wheat will be grown on the Prairies this year. The Minister of Agriculture smiles at me. He knows very well there will be wheat grown on the Prairies this year. Many thousands of acres of wheat will be grown in spite of this program. What other crops are the farmers going to turn to? What use will be made of the five million acreage reduction that took place last year and was presumably left fallow? Should the farmer turn to rape-seed? I will now deal with the rapeseed situation. Dr. A. M. Runciman, president of the Rapeseed Association of Canada said:
-that the world projection for the production of rapeseed is forecast to be 23 per cent higher than in 1969. This figure, he said, presumes only a slight increase on the part of Canadian farmers.
Traders, however, are expecting a 50 per cent acreage increase, Mr. Runciman said. Seed sales are up 30 per cent to 40 per cent and much of this seed is going into areas that never grew rapeseed before-areas in traditional wheat growing countries. Established growers will use their own seed and this has led the traders to forecast the 50 per cent increase.
Indications are, he said, that we had better get geared to moving the largest crop ever moved and at relatively low prices.
I am reading from the February 26 edition of the Manitoba Co-operator. This same paper has an article on flax. This article deals with a suggestion by Dr. W. J. Craddock, associate professor, Department of Agricultural Economics, University of Manitoba. It states:
While no estimates of carryover for the end of 1970-71 crop year could be made at this time, he said it should be noted that if 3,500,000 acres of flax were grown in 1970 even at an average yield of 11.5 bushels per acre, the total supply would be 50,500,000 bushels. If 25,400,000 bushels were, in fact, exported, 25,100,000 bushels would be available for domestic use or carryover...
... the maximum annual domestic use was 8,800,000 bushels and that was in 1956-57. In recent years this figure has been in the range of 4,000,000 to 6,000,000 bushels.
That shows the situation as far as flax is concerned. Should the farmer turn to oats and barley? I do not think I even have to read any comments on that except to prove the point I am making. In the Wheat Board's 1968 supplementary report, the latest available, it is shown that oats and barley produc-
March 2, 1970	COMMONS DEBATES	4265
tion have increased substantially. Although there has been some improvement in the movement of barley since that time, both these grains are in a heavy surplus position.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
One needs only look at production figures over the past decade to realize that our farmers have certainly solved the problems of production. However, when we turn to problems of merchandizing, transportation and distribution, an area in which the government should be deeply involved, we find we are barely out of the horse and buggy age. We were hamstrung initially by the inflexible marketing policy laid down by this government under which there was insistence on maintaining the IGA price long after our competitors had abandoned it. West Germany and Great Britain have been requesting a guaranteed protein content for the past six years but we have been content to continue a grading practice which is at least 30 years old.
This cavalier attitude toward the wishes of our customers, along with a determination to hold up the price of wheat in a buyers' market, has contributed to our loss of sales in traditional markets. At the best of times we must be competitive in price and quality, but in times of surplus we just cannot afford to be inflexible.
A recent article in the Globe and Mail had this to say with regard to our grading system:
Canadian wheat has been losing sales on the London market for reasons of quality and price, according to a consensus of dealers and millers ... A wheat board delegation spent nearly a week in London, assessing prospects in a market traditionally among Canada's best but which has been deteriorating over the past eight years.
The basic point to emerge from talks with the buyers and millers is that Canada's wheat export program has not adjusted to meet the changing demands of this market.
As a result, competitors-the Soviet Union and Australia-have been selling higher quality wheat at lower prices. Canadian sales have declined, though not drastically.
An explanation was offered in these words:
Canada was strongly criticized for being "the leading light for pressure to keep IGA prices at unrealistically high prices." In 1967, the Wheat Board was stuck with unrealistically high prices because, for political reasons, initial payments to farmers had been set too high.
Our farmers have demonstrated beyond doubt that they can produce a great variety of crops effectively. Farm production has 21701-59i
Wheat Acreage Reduction increased by more than 50 per cent in the last 20 years and this has been achieved by an agricultural labour force which has fallen by half in the same period. Unfortunately, our distribution and marketing system has failed to keep pace with this advance in production; it has changed very little in the last 20 years. Though our competitors have adopted protein content as a grading criterion, we still sell by bushel weight and colour.
The requirements of our customers have to be met, and we can do it because we still grow the best wheat in the world. We need to up-date our grading and to modernize our distribution system, including our port facilities, particularly on the west coast. We must do something about labour problems which have hampered the free flow of grain to customer countries. Lastly, we must try harder to meet competition. We must get out and sell. These things need to be done as quickly as possible if agriculture is to share the fruits of an affluent society.
In all fairness I would add that the minister's scheme is not without some compensatory features. It will provide employment for an army of inspectors who will be required to check wheat acreage and summer fallow against the quota books. It may help some of the larger farmers who will receive the maximum for summer fallow and be enabled to double production next year. But it will do little to alleviate the financial problem of the average farmer whose crop production is more diversified, particularly in areas where wheat production was already reduced by 26 per cent last year.
